implementation_notes: The contract declares MessageData<byte[]> (or string / a serializable reference type) and the framework does the Check Luggage work: the value is written to the configured repository before send and hydrated on consumption, so application code never stores or redeems the token itself. The repository is a strategy - InMemory, FileSystem, MongoDB GridFS, Azure Blob or any of them wrapped in EncryptedMessageDataRepository - while MessageDataDefaults.TimeToLive gives the payload a lifetime and Threshold plus AlwaysWriteToRepository=false lets small values travel inline.
pitfalls: MessageData<T> is a promise: reading .Value in a bus that was never configured with UseMessageData throws at consumption time, where it looks like a payload bug rather than a wiring bug.
AlwaysWriteToRepository defaults to true for backward compatibility, so even values below Threshold reach the repository unless the default is changed - blob storage fills up quietly.
The reference is part of the wire contract: producers and consumers must agree on the threshold and TTL settings, or a consumer that expects an inlined value receives a reference instead.

variants.name: Wolverine claim checks carried in the envelope header
variants.implementation_notes: Wolverine implements the same pattern with a different wire shape: the claim-check token travels in the message envelope header rather than inside the message body, so the contract record stays free of payload properties and broker tooling that surfaces headers can route, filter or expire on the token. The store is configured once on the transport, and handlers receive the hydrated value when they ask for it.
requires_features: a claim-check store configured on the transport
pitfalls: Header-carried tokens are invisible to a consumer that only deserializes bodies, so handlers that read raw JSON do not see the claim check at all.
Because the token is metadata, it is easy to log or forward it with tracing and thereby hand out access to the payload.

variants.name: Manual claim check: Blob upload plus a token in the queue message
variants.implementation_notes: When no messaging framework is in place, the pattern is written directly against the platform: upload the payload to Blob storage, send only the blob URL or key through Service Bus or Queue Storage (Event Grid can generate the token itself when it moves the blob), and let the consumer download and then delete the object. This is the shape shown in the Azure claim-check samples and is the right choice when the token must be visible to platform tooling such as Functions bindings or Event Grid subscriptions.
requires_features: Azure Service Bus or Queue Storage
variants.idiom_name: BlobClient.UploadAsync + ServiceBusMessage carrying the blob URI
pitfalls: The token is a URL, so anyone who can read the queue message can fetch the payload unless the container is private and the consumer authenticates with its own identity.
Deletion is not part of the transfer: without an explicit delete step (or a lifecycle rule) the container becomes an archive of every message ever sent.
Uploading before sending, or sending a token before the upload is committed, produces either orphaned blobs or messages whose payload does not exist.
